chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Usama Zayd al-Shammam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) stood at Mina when he had completed its rituals during the Farewell Hajj, so he said: 'O people! Listen to what I say to you and understand it from me, for I do not know, perhaps I will not meet you again at this standing place after our year.'

Then he said: 'Which day is greatest in sanctity?' They said, 'This day.' He said: 'So which month is greatest in sanctity?' They said, 'This month.' He said: 'So which city is greatest in sanctity?' They said, 'This city.'

He said: 'Indeed, your blood and your wealth are sacred upon you, like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours, until the day you meet Him, and He will question you about your deeds.'
'Indeed, have I delivered (the message)?' They said, 'Yes.'

He said: 'O Allah, bear witness! Indeed, whoever has an entrustment, let him return it to the one who entrusted it to him. For the blood of a Muslim and his wealth are not permissible except with his consent, and do not do injustice to yourselves, and do not return to disbelief after me.'
ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet say about the sanctity of blood and wealth in the Farewell Sermon?
ai.summary: Recorded in al-Kafi, this hadith captures the Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) Farewell Sermon at Mina, where he explicitly links the sanctity of life and wealth to the sacredness of the month and city, establishing a triad of inviolability. Shia scholars highlight this as a foundational text for *al-‘Adl* (divine justice) and *al-Tawhid* in social relations, emphasizing that injustice (*zulm*) is a return to pre-Islamic ignorance (*Jahiliyyah*). The narration serves as a comprehensive legal and ethical charter, reinforcing the Prophet’s final warning before his departure.
